title: After the Cuts: How Reduced Aid and Political Shifts Are Reshaping Global Health
label: 27 October 2026 · Global Health hearing
summary: Witnesses from Kenya, Zambia, Ethiopia, UNFPA, MSF and UK academic and research bodies described how rapid donor funding cuts—especially from US programmes—and rising political resistance to sexual and reproductive rights have harmed clinics, community services, data systems and research. They gave concrete examples of lost jobs and services, risks to children and to outbreak detection, and urged faster domestic funding, stronger local partnerships, protection of humanitarian and diagnostic capacity, and targeted UK action to support data, workforce and local civil society.

glossary.definition: Sexual and reproductive health and rights — services and policies that let people decide about sex, contraception, pregnancy and related health care.
United States Agency for International Development — a major US foreign aid agency funding health programmes.
The US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, a large donor programme for HIV/AIDS.
An international financing organisation that funds programmes for HIV, TB and malaria.
The UK-funded Women’s Integrated Sexual Health programme supporting family planning and sexual health services.
UK-funded programme that supported antimicrobial resistance (AMR) labs and surveillance in low- and middle-income countries.
Antimicrobial resistance — when bacteria or other microbes stop responding to treatments, making infections harder to treat.

chapters.title: Who spoke and the immediate shock
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses described sudden donor cuts—especially from US programmes—and how those shocks reached clinics, community workers and people living with HIV overnight.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are starting our inquiry into global health. Could each witness introduce themselves briefly?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: I run AYARHEP in Nairobi, a youth HIV organisation. We provide social support and link young people to the health system.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: I lead Copper Rose in Zambia. We work on youth reproductive and mental health and economic opportunities for women and young people.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: I am Executive Director of the Family Guidance Association of Ethiopia, working since 1966 across clinics, public, private and refugee services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Jerop, what did you see on the ground after the funding cuts?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: I’ve worked in HIV for a decade and live with HIV. Overnight young people panicked when US funding dropped—clinics and specialist community services were suddenly disrupted.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did the Kenyan Government have advance notice?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: No. We’d been in government committees on sustainability but none of us expected cuts to arrive so fast; neither did the Government appear prepared.

chapters.title: Concrete damage to services, jobs and data
chapters.takeaway: Cuts reduced community outreach and staffing, removed specialised clinics, and in places data systems and servers went offline, leaving people without medicines or follow-up.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia our outreach fell from 200,000 people a year to 45,000. Many standalone sexual health and DREAMS centres closed; community prevention disappeared.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: A modelling paper estimated 32,000 preventable deaths in three months after cuts, and 330,400 if disruptions continued over four years; children are hit especially hard.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: In Ethiopia our budget dropped by 40% in 2025. We lost 162 technical staff and withdrew from 366 public facilities. Teens share antiretrovirals in some places; contraceptive stockouts led to pregnancies and early marriage.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Committee was also told data systems were affected. What happened?

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: Some monitoring systems and patient data were hosted on US servers. When US funding stopped, access to those systems was lost, and many government data staff were laid off.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: It was said—rather bitterly—that DOGE wiped data that wasn’t theirs to delete.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Yes, and when you combine that with integration of services—pushing specialised HIV or youth services into general primary care—people get lost in the transition.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: Natasha, what does this mean for sustaining gains you’d made?

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: We’ve lost technical staff and momentum. Forecasting for drug procurement was disrupted and commodity pipelines are at risk; the policy work we’d driven has stalled without funding.

chapters.title: Politics, rights and the chilling effect
chapters.takeaway: Beyond money, political shifts narrowed what governments and organisations can say or do on sexual and reproductive rights, increasing stigma and cutting services.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: Have you faced ideological resistance to your work, and how can the UK help?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Yes. After public statements from leaders, language and services on rights were restricted. In Kenya, the word 'rights' or 'comprehensive sexuality education' became taboo; providers and clinics were attacked.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia similar shifts happened: 'rights' was stripped out of official discussion, 'gender' replaced with 'sex' in documents, and anti-CSE movements pushed back on school programmes. CSOs now spend more time fundraising than advocating.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: We also see foreign actors influencing policy and targeting parliamentarians, religious leaders and health staff with disinformation to roll back SRHR in the region.

turns.speaker: Tulip Siddiq
turns.text: How should the UK respond to ideological pressure?

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: The UK should use its diplomatic influence, publicly defend non-negotiable rights and support local civil society and accurate evidence to counter misinformation.

chapters.title: Research, labs and detecting new threats
chapters.takeaway: Cuts also hit research and laboratory networks, weakening tuberculosis care, antimicrobial resistance surveillance and outbreak detection.

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: Research projects often provided care and diagnostics. When grants stopped abruptly, clinical trials and treatment chains broke—raising risks of drug-resistant TB and more community transmission.

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: The Fleming Fund supported hundreds of labs; its reduction and other funding losses jeopardise surveillance and the ability to spot outbreaks quickly.

turns.speaker: David Taylor
turns.text: You mentioned delays in outbreak detection; can you give an example?

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: In one recent Ebola event an initial test for a different species returned negative, and sequencing two-and-a-half weeks later identified Ebola—an example of how weaker diagnostics and networks delay responses.

turns.speaker: Dr Kennedy Uadiale
turns.text: In Malawi the Fleming Fund withdrawal left labs without staff or supplies for months. Surveillance meetings stopped, and our ability to study decision-making on AMR weakened because the forums disappeared.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: How can the UK help on this research and lab front?

turns.speaker: Dr Kennedy Uadiale
turns.text: Champion affordable rapid AMR surveillance approaches, keep funding research partnerships, and support workforce and laboratory supplies so surveillance and quality of care continue.

chapters.title: Where to from here: practical fixes and UK choices
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses urged practical steps: protect humanitarian and diagnostic funding, fund local partners, invest in data and workforce, explore private sector and social insurance, and use UK diplomacy to defend rights.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: Are there any opportunities from these shocks?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: The shock forced governments to wake up and consider domestic financing and integration. But integration must be done gradually and funded, otherwise people get lost.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: Invest in data systems, digital training for community health workers, and involve the private sector and blended finance. Local organisations should get sustained funding—we remain on the ground regardless.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: Ethiopia is pursuing domestic resource mobilisation and some taxation to support emergency and SRHR programmes, plus private manufacturing partnerships and cross-subsidy models at NGOs.

turns.speaker: Dr Kirrily de Polnay
turns.text: From MSF’s view: protect humanitarian funding and upstream prevention—if basic services fail children and mothers end up needing much more complex and costly hospital care.

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: UNFPA asks the UK to keep funding supplies and use its multilateral influence to support maternal health, defend rights, and press multilaterals to channel funds to local partners.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A final point on UK policy: is concentrating ODA through multilaterals a problem?

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: If it reduces bilateral research partnerships and university links, it hurts long-term scientist-to-scientist capacity building and training of the next generation.

turns.speaker: Dr Kirrily de Polnay
turns.text: Multilaterals matter, but many fragile contexts still need direct support and accountability; donors should ensure money reaches local needs quickly and transparently.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. We will follow up with written questions. Please pass on our thanks to your teams for the work you do in very difficult circumstances.
